topicName: Analyzing OOM Kills and Kernel Panics
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Analyzing OOM Kills and Kernel Panics in Docker"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When running production workloads in Docker containers, unexpected terminations can destabilize your architecture. Understanding how to diagnose Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kills and kernel panics is critical for maintaining high availability."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Docker OOM Kills"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"An OOM kill occurs when a process inside a container exceeds its allocated memory limit. The Linux kernel's OOM killer steps in and terminates the offending process to protect the host system from crashing entirely."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Containers typically exit with code 137 when they are OOM killed."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Code 137 translates to 128 + 9 (SIGKILL signal)."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Diagnosing OOM Kills on the Host"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"To confirm whether a container was terminated due to an OOM event, inspect the Docker daemon logs or the host kernel ring buffer using system utilities."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"docker inspect --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}' <container_name_or_id>"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can also search system logs directly on the host using dmesg to view the exact memory exhaustion details."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"dmesg -T | grep -i oom"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Investigating Kernel Panics"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike OOM kills, which usually only terminate a specific container or process, a kernel panic forces an immediate and unrecoverable shutdown of the entire operating system kernel. While rare within standard unprivileged containers (unless running with privileged flags or modifying host kernel parameters), kernel panics affect the entire Docker host."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Check host system logs in /var/log/syslog or /var/log/messages for panic signatures."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Review crash dumps if kdump is configured on the host machine."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Preventive Strategies"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"To prevent unexpected OOM terminations, always configure explicit memory limits and reservations when starting your Docker containers."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"docker run -d --name my_app -m 512m --memory-swap 512m nginx"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"By setting matching memory and swap limits, you prevent the container from swapping to disk, ensuring predictable performance and clear OOM boundaries."}]
